title: Fourier Series
tagline: Every repeating signal is a chord — here's how to read the notes.
description: From periodic functions to the frequency domain. The one move that matters — extracting a coefficient by integrating against a basis function — gets the depth; the rest is calibrated refresher for an engineer who has seen this before.

intro.hook: Any repeating signal — a violin note, a heartbeat, a year of temperatures — is a sum of simple waves.
body: The claim sounds too strong the first time you hear it. Take any periodic signal, however jagged: a square wave with vertical cliffs, the sawtooth buzz of a synthesiser, the trace of a beating heart. Fourier's assertion is that each one is nothing but pure sine waves added together, and that you can find exactly how much of each.

It was controversial precisely because it seemed impossible — Lagrange objected that smooth curves could never build a corner. He was almost right; the way the sum behaves at a jump is subtle enough to have its own name and its own century of argument.
Once you accept it, you gain a second way of seeing everything. Every signal has a shape in time and a shape in frequency, and problems that are hopeless in one are often trivial in the other.

why.title: It runs the modern world
why.text: MP3, JPEG, MRI, Wi-Fi, noise cancellation and spectrum analysis are all this one idea, industrialised.

why.title: A second pair of eyes
why.text: Switching between time and frequency turns hard problems into easy ones — differentiation becomes multiplication.

why.title: Where filtering comes from
why.text: Bass, treble, smoothing and denoising all mean the same thing: keep some frequencies, discard others.

intro.closer: Fourier was trying to understand heat. He ended up handing us the format of nearly every sound and picture you will see today.

concepts.title: Periodic functions and superposition
concepts.summary: A function with period T repeats forever; Fourier's claim is that any reasonable one is a sum of sines and cosines at the fundamental frequency and its integer multiples.

cards.md:
A function is **periodic with period T** if f(x + T) = f(x) for all x. Sines, cosines, square waves, heartbeats, seasonal patterns — anything that repeats.

Fourier's 1807 claim, scandalous at the time: **any reasonable periodic function is a sum of sines and cosines** — even ones with corners and jumps, which look nothing like smooth waves.

## f(x) = a₀/2 + Σₙ₌₁^∞ [aₙ cos(nωx) + bₙ sin(nωx)]

where ω = 2π/T is the **fundamental frequency** and the n-th term — the **n-th harmonic** — completes exactly n cycles per period. Lagrange objected that a sum of smooth waves could never make a corner. He was wrong, in an interesting way (that's the Gibbs concept, ahead).

You saw this machinery in the early '70s. The plan here: sprint through what re-recognition handles, then slow down hard on the one move everything hinges on — how orthogonality (perpendicularity, generalized to functions) lets you fish out a single coefficient.

Why sums? Because the systems Fourier cared about (heat flow, vibration) are **linear**: if f and g are solutions, so is any combination αf + βg. Solve for each pure sine, add up the pieces — superposition does the rest.

The load-bearing shift in viewpoint: treat functions as **vectors**. A vector in 3-space is a weighted sum of basis vectors ê₁, ê₂, ê₃. A periodic function is a weighted sum of basis *functions* — 1, cos(ωx), sin(ωx), cos(2ωx), sin(2ωx), … An infinite-dimensional space, but the same geometry.

Two questions then decide everything:

1. Is this basis *orthogonal*, so components can be read off independently? (Yes — next concept.)
2. Do the sums actually converge back to f? (Mostly yes, with one famous ~9% asterisk.)

Every coefficient formula you half-remember is just 'take the dot product with a basis vector,' dressed up in integrals.

questions.prompt: A signal has period T = 2 ms. Its third harmonic completes how many cycles in one period, at what frequency?
options: 1 cycle, at 500 Hz
3 cycles, at 1500 Hz
3 cycles, at 500 Hz
1/3 cycle, at 167 Hz
feedback: That's the fundamental (n = 1). The n-th harmonic runs n times faster than the fundamental.
Right — fundamental is 1/T = 500 Hz; the third harmonic fits 3 full cycles per period, so 1500 Hz.
Three cycles per period means three times the fundamental frequency, not the same frequency.
Harmonics are integer *multiples* of the fundamental, never fractions — a 1/3-cycle wave wouldn't repeat with period T.

questions.prompt: Why does the Fourier recipe only use frequencies ω, 2ω, 3ω, … and not, say, 1.5ω?
options: Non-integer multiples are too hard to integrate
A component at 1.5ω doesn't repeat with period T, so the sum would no longer be T-periodic
1.5ω terms are always zero anyway
It's a convention; any frequencies would work equally well
feedback: The integrals are no harder — the issue is periodicity, not computability.
Right. sin(1.5ωx) needs 2T to repeat; adding it breaks the period. Only integer multiples of ω share period T.
They're not automatically zero — they're *excluded* because they'd wreck the periodicity.
Not a convention: the harmonics at nω are exactly the sinusoids that repeat every T. That set is forced.

questions.prompt: The whole strategy of Fourier series treats functions as vectors. What plays the role of the basis vectors?
options: The coefficients aₙ and bₙ
The values f(x₁), f(x₂), … at sample points
The functions 1, cos(nωx), sin(nωx)
The period T and its multiples
feedback: The coefficients are the *components* along each basis direction — the weights, not the basis.
Sample values are more like coordinates in the 'standard basis' of points; Fourier's insight is to change to a smarter basis.
Right — sines and cosines are the basis directions; aₙ, bₙ are how far f extends along each one.
T sets the fundamental frequency but isn't itself a direction in function space.

concepts.title: Orthogonality: a dot product for functions
concepts.summary: ⟨f,g⟩ = ∫f(x)g(x)dx over one period acts as a dot product, and the sine/cosine family is mutually orthogonal under it — the fact the whole subject stands on.

cards.h: From Σ to ∫: the dot product generalizes
cards.md:
For vectors, the dot product is a sum of products of matching components: **a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ**. Orthogonal means it's zero.

Now let the 'components' of a function be its values at every point. The sum over components becomes an integral:

## ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫ f(x)g(x) dx  (over one period)

This behaves exactly like a dot product: it's linear, symmetric, and ⟨f, f⟩ = ∫f² ≥ 0 acts as squared length. Two functions are **orthogonal** when ⟨f, g⟩ = 0.

Don't read this as a formal analogy — it's the literal geometry of function space. 'Perpendicular functions' means: multiply them pointwise, integrate over a period, get zero. Every projection trick you know from vectors now transfers wholesale.

cards.h: The trig family is mutually orthogonal
cards.md:
Over one period, say [−π, π], the basis functions are pairwise orthogonal:

- ∫ sin(mx) cos(nx) dx = 0 — **always** (odd × even is odd: the integrand cancels itself)
- ∫ cos(mx) cos(nx) dx = 0 for m ≠ n
- ∫ sin(mx) sin(nx) dx = 0 for m ≠ n

Why do mismatched frequencies cancel? Product-to-sum: cos(mx)cos(nx) = ½[cos((m−n)x) + cos((m+n)x)]. For m ≠ n both terms are genuine oscillations, and any whole number of cosine cycles integrates to zero — equal area above and below.

But when **m = n**, the first term becomes cos(0) = 1 — a constant that *doesn't* cancel:

## ∫₋π^π cos²(nx) dx = ∫₋π^π sin²(nx) dx = π

That's the whole mechanism: mismatched frequencies beat against each other and average away; a frequency multiplied by *itself* rectifies into something with a nonzero mean. Matching survives, everything else dies.

Recall how you read off a component of a vector: v = v₁ê₁ + v₂ê₂ + v₃ê₃, and because the basis is orthonormal (mutually perpendicular and unit-length), **v·ê₂ = v₂**. The dot product with ê₂ annihilates every term except the ê₂ one.

Same move in function space. Take f = a₀/2 + Σ[aₙcos(nx) + bₙsin(nx)], multiply the *whole series* by cos(3x), integrate over a period. Term by term:

- every sin term dies (sin ⊥ cos, always)
- every cos(nx) with n ≠ 3 dies (mismatched frequencies)
- the constant dies (a cosine integrates to zero over full cycles)
- **one term survives**: a₃ ∫cos²(3x)dx = a₃π

So ∫f(x)cos(3x)dx = a₃π, and a₃ falls out. One integral, one coefficient, no simultaneous equations — an infinite system of unknowns solved one at a time, independently.

This is the concept to actually re-own. The coefficient formulas in the next concept are not new facts to memorize; they are this projection, written out.

questions.prompt: Without computing: ∫₋π^π sin(3x)cos(5x) dx = ?
options: π
0, but only because 3 ≠ 5
0, because sin × cos gives an odd integrand over a symmetric interval — regardless of the frequencies
feedback: π is what you get when a function meets *itself* — sin(3x) against sin(3x). Mismatched pairs give zero.
It is zero, but for a stronger reason: sin ⊥ cos even when m = n. ∫sin(3x)cos(3x)dx = 0 too.
Right — odd × even = odd, which integrates to zero on [−π, π]. The sine-cosine cross terms vanish for *every* m, n.
No mismatched product of basis sinusoids leaves a residue — orthogonality forces exactly zero.

questions.prompt: You multiply the full Fourier series of f by sin(2x) and integrate over [−π, π]. What survives, and why?
options: Only b₂∫sin²(2x)dx = b₂π — every other term is orthogonal to sin(2x)
All the bₙ terms — sines match sines
The b₂ and a₂ terms — anything at frequency 2 survives
Nothing — you need cos to extract coefficients
feedback: Right. This is the extraction move: the integral acts as a dot product with sin(2x), and only the parallel component survives.
sin(nx) with n ≠ 2 is orthogonal to sin(2x) — mismatched frequencies beat and average to zero. Only n = 2 lives.
a₂cos(2x) dies too: sin(2x)cos(2x) = ½sin(4x), which integrates to zero. Frequency match isn't enough — phase (sin vs cos) must match as well.
Sines extract the bₙ exactly as cosines extract the aₙ. The machinery is symmetric.

questions.prompt: What is the deepest reason Fourier coefficients can be computed one at a time, each ignoring all the others?
options: The series converges fast, so later terms don't matter
The basis functions are orthogonal, so each coefficient is an independent projection
Sines and cosines are bounded by 1
Integration is a linear operation
feedback: Convergence speed is irrelevant here — the projection is exact even for slowly converging series.
Right. Orthogonality decouples the infinite system: ⟨f, basisₙ⟩ touches only coefficient n. Non-orthogonal bases would need solving all equations simultaneously.
Boundedness keeps things finite but does nothing to separate one coefficient from another.
Linearity is necessary (it lets you integrate term by term) but not sufficient — without orthogonality the cross terms wouldn't vanish.

concepts.title: Computing the coefficients
concepts.summary: aₙ and bₙ are projections: integrate f against the matching basis function over one period, divide by the basis function's squared length. Symmetry halves the work.

cards.h: The formulas, and where they come from
cards.md:
For period 2L, write f(x) = a₀/2 + Σ[aₙcos(nπx/L) + bₙsin(nπx/L)]. The extraction move from the last concept, done for every n at once:

## aₙ = (1/L) ∫₋L^L f(x) cos(nπx/L) dx
## bₙ = (1/L) ∫₋L^L f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx

The 1/L is not decoration — it's dividing by the squared length of the basis function (∫cos² over the period = L). Projection = dot product ÷ ‖basis‖².

Two conventions worth re-fixing:

- **Why a₀/2?** So the aₙ formula works for n = 0 too (∫1²dx = 2L, twice the others). The constant term a₀/2 is just the **average value of f** — its DC (direct-current) level.
- On [−π, π], L = π and these reduce to the (1/π)∫f cos(nx)dx you likely remember.

Before integrating anything, check symmetry — it can kill half the coefficients on sight.

- **f even** (f(−x) = f(x)): f × sin is odd → every **bₙ = 0**. Cosines only.
- **f odd** (f(−x) = −f(x)): f × cos is odd → every **aₙ = 0**, including the average. Sines only.

Makes sense: cosines are even, sines are odd; a function can only be built from bricks that share its symmetry.

And for the survivors, integrate over half the period and double:

## f odd: bₙ = (2/L) ∫₀^L f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx

One symmetry glance can turn a page of integration into three lines. The examiners of 1973 knew this; so should the you of now.

The canonical example — f(x) = −1 on (−π, 0), +1 on (0, π), repeating with period 2π.

f is **odd** → all aₙ = 0 instantly. For the sines:

bₙ = (2/π) ∫₀^π (1)·sin(nx) dx = (2/π) · [(1 − cos(nπ))/n]

cos(nπ) alternates: −1 for odd n, +1 for even n. So 1 − cos(nπ) is 2 or 0:

## bₙ = 4/(nπ) for odd n,  0 for even n

## f(x) = (4/π)[sin x + sin(3x)/3 + sin(5x)/5 + …]

Read the result, don't just verify it:

- **Only odd harmonics.** The square wave has an extra symmetry (each half-period is the negative of the previous), and even harmonics can't have it.
- **Amplitudes fall off as 1/n** — slowly. That slow decay is the price of the jump discontinuities, a thread the next two concepts pull hard.

questions.prompt: f(x) = x on (−π, π), extended periodically (the sawtooth). Before computing anything, what do you know?
options: All bₙ = 0 — cosines only
All aₙ = 0 including the average — sines only
Only that a₀ = 0
Nothing until you integrate
feedback: That's the rule for an *even* function. x is odd: x(−x)… check: f(−x) = −x = −f(x).
Right — f(x) = x is odd, so it's built purely from odd bricks: sines. Every cosine integral is odd × even = odd → zero.
True but weak — oddness kills every aₙ, not just the average.
Symmetry is exactly the thing that lets you know before integrating. Never skip the parity check.

questions.prompt: For the ±1 square wave, b₁ = 4/π ≈ 1.27 — the fundamental's amplitude *exceeds* the wave's own height of 1. How?
options: It's an error — no component can exceed the signal
The higher harmonics partially cancel the fundamental's excess, flattening the peak into the plateau
The 4/π is a normalization artifact with no physical meaning
Square waves are a pathological case where Fourier fails
feedback: Components aren't slices of the signal's height — they can overshoot as long as the others correct for it.
Right. sin(3x)/3 is *negative* near the fundamental's peak — the harmonics shave the crest and fill the shoulders to build the flat top.
4/π is the honest physical amplitude of the 1st harmonic — pass the square wave through a narrow filter at ω and that's what comes out.
Nothing pathological: the series converges to the square wave everywhere except the jump points.

questions.prompt: A signal rides on a nonzero baseline: f(x) = 3 + (periodic wiggle averaging zero). Which coefficient captures the 3?
options: b₀
a₁
a₀/2 — the constant term is the mean of f over a period
None — you must subtract the baseline before using Fourier
feedback: There is no b₀ — sin(0·x) = 0 identically; it can't carry anything.
a₁ is the cos(ωx) component — it oscillates and averages to zero, so it can't hold a DC level.
Right. a₀/2 = (1/2L)∫f dx = the average value. Engineers call it the DC component for exactly this reason.
No preprocessing needed — the constant basis function 1 is part of the family and soaks up the mean automatically.

concepts.title: Convergence and the Gibbs phenomenon
concepts.summary: At a jump the series converges to the midpoint, and partial sums forever overshoot by ~9% of the jump — the spike narrows but never shrinks.

cards.md:
Does the infinite sum actually equal f? For any piecewise-smooth function (finitely many jumps and corners per period — every signal you'll meet), the **Dirichlet conditions** settle it:

- At every point where f is continuous: the series converges to **f(x)**. ✓
- At a jump: the series converges to the **midpoint** of the jump — (f(x⁻) + f(x⁺))/2 — *regardless of what value you assigned f at that point*.

The midpoint rule isn't arbitrary. The series is built from symmetric, democratic ingredients; asked to pick a value inside a jump it has no basis to favor either side, so it splits the difference.

Check it on the square wave at x = 0: every term sin(n·0) = 0, so the series says f(0) = 0 — exactly halfway between −1 and +1.

cards.h: Gibbs: the overshoot that never dies
cards.md:
Now the famous asterisk. Truncate the square-wave series at N terms and plot it. Near each jump the partial sum **overshoots** — a spike past the true level, then a decaying ripple.

The natural expectation: more terms → smaller overshoot. **False.** As N grows:

- the spike gets **narrower** (it hugs the jump ever more tightly),
- but its **height converges to ≈ 8.9% of the jump size** — and stays there. Forever.

For the ±1 square wave (jump of 2), the partial sums keep peaking near 1.18 no matter how many thousands of terms you add.

The number is universal: (2/π)∫₀^π (sin t)/t dt ≈ 1.1789 of the half-jump — the Wilbraham–Gibbs constant. Every jump discontinuity, any function, same 9%.

Sounds like a contradiction: the series converges at every point, yet the overshoot never shrinks?

Resolution: the spike doesn't sit still — it **migrates toward the jump** as N grows. Pick any fixed x near the jump: eventually the spike moves inside your position, and the partial sums at *your* x settle down to f(x). Pointwise, all is well. But at every stage there is always *some* x (ever closer to the jump) currently under the spike.

This is the textbook gap between **pointwise** convergence (each fixed x eventually behaves) and **uniform** convergence (the worst error over all x goes to zero). Fourier series of discontinuous functions converge pointwise, never uniformly.

This isn't an academic curiosity. Truncating a spectrum (the signal's frequency content) is what every band-limited channel (frequencies capped below a cutoff), every low-pass filter (passes only low frequencies), every JPEG (lossy image compression) does — and Gibbs is the **ringing** at sharp edges that engineers have fought ever since: pre-echo in audio, halos at image edges. Lagrange was almost right — the corner is achieved only in the limit, and the 9% ghost of his objection haunts every finite approximation.

questions.prompt: A periodic f has f(x⁻) = 2 and f(x⁺) = 6 at a jump, and the textbook defines f(x) = 6 there. The Fourier series at x converges to:
options: 6 — the defined value
2 — the left limit
4 — the midpoint of the jump
It diverges at jump points
feedback: The series never sees the single-point definition — changing f at one point changes no integral, hence no coefficient.
The series is symmetric between the two sides; it has no reason to favor the left.
Right: (2 + 6)/2 = 4. The coefficients only know f through integrals, and integrals can't distinguish single-point values.
It converges fine at jumps — just to the midpoint rather than either side.

questions.prompt: You sum 10,000 terms of the square-wave series instead of 100. What happens to the Gibbs overshoot near the jump?
options: Its height shrinks toward zero — that's what convergence means
It narrows, but its height still approaches ~9% of the jump
It grows without bound
It disappears exactly at N = 1/(jump size)
feedback: The seductive wrong answer — pointwise convergence does NOT force the peak down; it only forces the spike to migrate toward the jump.
Right. Height → the Wilbraham–Gibbs level (≈ 1.18 for a ±1 wave), width → 0. More terms buy narrowness, never a shorter spike.
It's bounded — the overshoot converges to the ~9% level from whichever side, it doesn't blow up.
There's no magic N; the overshoot persists at every finite truncation.

questions.prompt: A digital scope shows ripples ('ringing') just before and after each edge of a measured square pulse. The Fourier explanation:
options: The instrument's bandwidth truncates the spectrum — a partial Fourier sum, so Gibbs oscillation appears at the jumps
Electrical noise happens to concentrate at edges
The pulse itself physically rings; the scope is faithful
Aliasing from sampling too slowly
feedback: Right. Finite bandwidth = keeping only harmonics below a cutoff = a truncated Fourier series — and truncation at a jump manufactures the Gibbs ripple.
Noise is broadband and random; Gibbs ringing is deterministic, symmetric, and always pinned to the discontinuities.
Possible in some circuits, but the universal edge-ripple on band-limited instruments is the mathematics of truncation, present even with a perfect source.
Aliasing folds high frequencies into wrong low ones — a different artifact. Ringing at edges is the signature of a chopped spectrum.

concepts.title: The complex form
concepts.summary: cₙ = (1/2π)∫f(x)e^(−inx)dx repackages each (aₙ, bₙ) pair into one complex number holding amplitude and phase. Bookkeeping, not new mathematics.

cards.md:
Euler's formula, e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ, runs both ways:

cos(nx) = (e^(inx) + e^(−inx))/2   sin(nx) = (e^(inx) − e^(−inx))/(2i)

Substitute into the series and regroup by exponentials. The three families (constant, cosines, sines) collapse into **one**:

## f(x) = Σₙ₌₋∞^∞ cₙ e^(inx)
## cₙ = (1/2π) ∫₋π^π f(x) e^(−inx) dx

One formula, indexed over all integers — negative n included. Orthogonality becomes a single clean statement: ∫e^(imx)e^(−inx)dx = 0 unless m = n (then 2π). The extraction move survives intact: multiply by e^(−inx), integrate, one term lives.

Nothing new was learned about f — the information was repackaged. The dictionary:

- **c₀ = a₀/2** — still the average
- **cₙ = (aₙ − i·bₙ)/2** for n > 0
- **c₋ₙ = (aₙ + i·bₙ)/2 = c̄ₙ** (complex conjugate) when f is real

Two real sequences became one complex sequence with a symmetry constraint. Same degrees of freedom, zero new content.

Why bother? The complex form is where the *useful* structure lives:

- **|cₙ| = ½√(aₙ² + bₙ²)** — half the amplitude of harmonic n
- **arg(cₙ)** — its phase

Amplitude-and-phase is how engineers actually think about harmonics, and a single complex number carries both. Bonus: differentiation becomes multiplication — d/dx turns cₙ into in·cₙ. That one-liner (derivatives → multiplication by frequency) is why the complex form owns signal processing and PDE-solving (partial differential equations) alike.

The index n now runs over negative integers — is something spinning backward?

For a real signal: no physics, pure bookkeeping. e^(inx) is a phasor (a complex-plane vector) rotating counterclockwise; e^(−inx) rotates clockwise. A real cosine is the *sum of both*:

cos(nx) = ½e^(inx) + ½e^(−inx)

Two counter-rotating phasors whose imaginary parts cancel at every instant — that's the only way to build a purely real oscillation out of complex exponentials. The negative-frequency coefficient c₋ₙ = c̄ₙ carries no independent information; it's the mirror half that keeps the sum real.

So when a spectrum plot shows symmetric spikes at ±n: that's one physical oscillation, drawn in a basis that splits it into two rotations. (For genuinely complex signals — I/Q data (in-phase/quadrature) in radio, analytic signals — the two sides *do* become independent. Same formalism, more room.)

questions.prompt: f is a real signal with c₅ = 0.3 − 0.4i. What is c₋₅?
options: 0.3 + 0.4i — the complex conjugate
−0.3 + 0.4i — the negative
0.3 − 0.4i — the same value
Undetermined without more information
feedback: Right — realness of f forces c₋ₙ = c̄ₙ. The negative side of the spectrum is the conjugate mirror of the positive side.
That's −c₅; the reality constraint conjugates, it doesn't negate. The imaginary parts must cancel in the sum, not the whole coefficients.
Equal coefficients would make the sine parts add instead of cancel — the imaginary content of f wouldn't vanish.
It IS determined: for real f the two halves of the spectrum are locked together by conjugate symmetry.

questions.prompt: Does the complex form encode information about f that the aₙ, bₙ form misses?
options: Yes — the phases arg(cₙ) are new information
Yes — negative frequencies add content
No — cₙ = (aₙ − i·bₙ)/2 is an invertible repackaging; same information, tighter notation
No — but only for even functions
feedback: The phase was always there — hidden in the *ratio* of bₙ to aₙ (a cos + b sin = A cos(nx − φ)). The complex form displays it; it doesn't create it.
For real f, c₋ₙ is fully determined by cₙ — the negative side is a mirror, not a new channel.
Right. It's a change of coordinates in coefficient space: two reals (aₙ, bₙ) ↔ one complex cₙ. Bookkeeping, chosen because algebra (especially d/dx → ×in) gets dramatically cleaner.
The equivalence holds for every function, even or not — parity affects which coefficients vanish, not the translatability.

questions.prompt: In the complex form, what happens to the Fourier coefficients when you differentiate f?
options: cₙ → cₙ/(in) — differentiation divides by frequency
cₙ → in·cₙ — each harmonic is multiplied by its frequency (times i)
The coefficients are unchanged; only the basis changes
You must recompute all integrals from scratch
feedback: Dividing by in is *integration* — the inverse operation. Differentiation amplifies high frequencies, so it must multiply by n, not divide.
Right: d/dx e^(inx) = in·e^(inx), so each coefficient just picks up a factor of in. Calculus becomes algebra — the core reason PDEs surrender to Fourier methods.
The basis functions e^(inx) are eigenfunctions of d/dx — the basis survives; the coefficients are what change (by the eigenvalue in).
That's exactly the labor the complex form abolishes: differentiate term by term, and each term is trivial.

concepts.title: The spectrum view of signals
concepts.summary: The coefficients ARE the signal, re-described: |cₙ| against n is its spectrum. Smoothness in time is decay in frequency — sharp edges demand strong high harmonics.

cards.md:
You now hold two complete descriptions of any periodic signal:

- **Time domain**: f(x) — its value at every instant
- **Frequency domain**: the list of coefficients — how much of each harmonic it contains

Neither is more real. The **spectrum** — amplitude Aₙ = √(aₙ² + bₙ²) (or 2|cₙ|) plotted against n — is the frequency-domain portrait.

Read the square wave's spectrum: bars at n = 1, 3, 5, 7… with heights (4/π)·(1, 1/3, 1/5, 1/7…). Silence at even n. That bar chart *is* the square wave, as completely as its graph is.

The physical meaning of bar n is concrete: pass the signal through a filter that keeps only frequency n·f₀, and a sine of exactly that amplitude and phase comes out. A prism does this to light; a cochlea does it to sound; a spectrum analyzer does it to anything. Your ear literally hears the spectrum, not the waveform — which is why a violin and a flute playing the same A₄ sound different: same fundamental, different bar heights.

Why does the square wave need harmonics all the way up, and why do they fade so slowly (1/n)?

A harmonic at frequency n can't change faster than its own oscillation. To build a **jump** — an instantaneous change — no finite collection of speed-limited waves suffices; you need contributions from arbitrarily high frequencies, and lots of them.

The general law: **smoothness in time ⇔ decay rate in frequency.**

- Jump discontinuity → coefficients ~ 1/n (square wave, sawtooth)
- Continuous but kinked → ~ 1/n² (triangle wave)
- Each additional continuous derivative buys one more power of 1/n
- Infinitely smooth → decay faster than any power

This is a diagnostic you can run in both directions: see a spectrum falling as 1/n², and you know the waveform has corners but no jumps — without ever seeing it. And it prices things: sharp edges cost bandwidth. A crisp pulse over a narrow channel is a contradiction; every communication system lives inside that constraint.

cards.h: Parseval: energy is conserved across the views
cards.md:
The two portraits agree about energy. **Parseval's theorem**:

## (1/2π) ∫₋π^π |f(x)|² dx = Σₙ₌₋∞^∞ |cₙ|²

The mean power of the signal equals the sum of the powers of its harmonics. Changing basis rotated the vector; orthogonality means nothing leaked and nothing double-counted — it's the Pythagorean theorem in function space (‖v‖² = Σ components², in any orthonormal basis).

This makes the spectrum an **energy budget**. For the square wave, the fundamental alone carries (4/π)²/2 ≈ 0.81 of the unit power — 81%. Fundamental plus third harmonic: ~90%. The infinite tail of higher harmonics splits the last few percent — which is exactly why a low-pass-filtered square wave still looks recognizably square (Gibbs ripple aside): most of the *energy* was in the low bars all along, even though the *sharpness* lived in the high ones.

questions.prompt: In the ±1 square wave's spectrum, the bar at n = 5 has height 4/5π. What does that number physically mean?
options: The signal spends 4/5π of its time at frequency 5f₀
A filter passing only 5f₀ would output a sine of amplitude 4/5π
The square wave's value at x = 5
The probability that the signal contains frequency 5f₀
feedback: Signals don't take turns being frequencies — all harmonics are present simultaneously, at all times.
Right — the coefficient is the literal amplitude of the sinusoid you'd extract with an ideal narrowband filter at 5f₀. Measurable on a bench.
The spectrum's axis is frequency index n, not position x. The two portraits have different axes entirely.
Nothing probabilistic here — the harmonic content is deterministic and exact.

questions.prompt: Signal A's coefficients decay like 1/n; signal B's like 1/n³. Without seeing either waveform, what can you say?
options: A is smoother than B
B has jump discontinuities; A doesn't
A has jumps; B is continuous with at least a continuous first derivative — B is markedly smoother
Nothing — decay rate and smoothness are unrelated
feedback: Backwards — slower decay means more high-frequency content, which means *less* smooth. 1/n is the roughest of the standard decays.
Reversed: 1/n decay is the fingerprint of jumps. B's fast decay rules jumps out.
Right. 1/n ⇒ jumps (square/sawtooth class); 1/n³ ⇒ continuous, with continuous f′ as well. The decay exponent is a smoothness meter you can read off a spectrum analyzer.
They're tightly coupled — smoothness in time IS decay in frequency; that equivalence is the concept's core law.

questions.prompt: You low-pass a square wave, keeping only harmonics 1 and 3. Per Parseval, the output retains ~90% of the power. What did the missing 10% mostly carry?
options: The signal's average level
The edges — the sharpness of the transitions
The fundamental pitch
Nothing important; the last 10% is noise
feedback: The average is c₀ (zero here anyway) and passes any low-pass filter untouched.
Right — high harmonics contribute little energy but ALL the fast structure. The output is recognizably square-ish yet visibly rounded at the transitions. Energy lives low; sharpness lives high.
The pitch is harmonic 1 — kept, and carrying 81% of the power by itself.
It's not noise — it's exactly the deterministic high-frequency content that built the edges. Lose it and the edges slump.

concepts.title: Toward the Fourier transform
concepts.summary: Let the period grow without bound: harmonic spacing shrinks to zero, the discrete spectrum melts into a continuous one, and the series becomes the Fourier transform.

cards.md:
Fourier series demand periodicity — but a single voltage spike, a lone pulse, a one-off transient never repeats. How do you take the spectrum of something that happens once?

The trick: a non-repeating signal is a periodic signal whose **period is infinite**. So take a pulse, pretend it repeats every T, compute the series, and watch what happens as T → ∞.

The harmonics sit at frequencies n·(2π/T) — spaced **Δω = 2π/T apart**. As T grows:

- T = 1 s → lines every 2π rad/s
- T = 1 hour → lines packed 3600× tighter
- T → ∞ → the lines **merge into a continuum**

The discrete bar chart of cₙ melts into a smooth curve over all frequencies. Every frequency now participates, not just integer multiples of a fundamental — because with no repetition, there is no fundamental.

Chase the limit carefully (each cₙ shrinks like 1/T, so track T·cₙ — a *density* per unit frequency) and the series pair becomes the **transform pair**:

## F(ω) = ∫₋∞^∞ f(x) e^(−iωx) dx
## f(x) = (1/2π) ∫₋∞^∞ F(ω) e^(iωx) dω

Nothing structurally new — inspect the anatomy:

- F(ω) is the cₙ formula with the discrete n·ω₀ replaced by a continuous ω: still *the dot product of f against a complex exponential* — the same extraction move from concept 2, now asked at every real frequency.
- The reconstruction is the series with Σ → ∫: superpose the basis functions, weighted by their coefficients.

Everything you built transfers: conjugate symmetry for real signals, d/dx → ×iω, Parseval (∫|f|² ∝ ∫|F|²), smoothness ⇔ decay. One new headline: **a narrow pulse has a wide spectrum, and vice versa** — sharpness in time and concentration in frequency are enemies. Pushed to the limit, that trade-off is the uncertainty principle.

You're standing at a three-way junction:

**PDEs** (your next topic, and the one you solved in '73-'74): separation of variables turns the heat and wave equations into ODEs (ordinary differential equations) *per harmonic* — Fourier coefficients evolve independently because e^(inx) are eigenfunctions (functions an operator only scales) of d²/dx². Fourier invented the series for exactly this. The heat equation's answer: harmonic n decays like e^(−n²kt) — high frequencies die fastest, which is why sharp temperature profiles blur smooth. Diffusion is a low-pass filter.

**Computation**: sample the signal and the transform becomes the DFT (Discrete Fourier Transform) — computable for N points in N log N steps by the **FFT** (Fast Fourier Transform; Cooley-Tukey, 1965 — it arrived after your coursework, and it's why the frequency domain went from theory to the default engineering habitat). Every audio codec, image compressor, and spectrum analyzer runs on it.

**The habit of mind**: 'what does this look like in the frequency domain?' is a permanent addition to the toolkit — filtering is multiplication, convolution (a sliding overlap of two signals) collapses, cycles hiding in noisy series show themselves. Whenever a problem involves anything that repeats, oscillates, or diffuses, change basis first and ask again.

questions.prompt: As the assumed period T of a signal grows, the spacing between adjacent harmonics in its spectrum:
options: Grows proportionally to T
Shrinks as 2π/T, so the spectral lines crowd toward a continuum
Stays fixed — spacing depends only on the signal's shape
Oscillates depending on the harmonics present
feedback: Inverted — a *longer* period means a *lower* fundamental, hence lines packed closer, not farther.
Right. Δω = 2π/T → 0 as T → ∞. The continuum limit of that crowding is exactly the Fourier transform.
Spacing is set purely by the period (Δω = 2π/T), not by the waveform within it — shape sets the heights, period sets the grid.
The grid of possible frequencies is rigid at multiples of 2π/T; only the amplitudes on the grid depend on the shape.

questions.prompt: In the T → ∞ limit, the Fourier coefficient cₙ corresponds to what feature of the transform F(ω)?
options: F(ω) is a density: cₙ ≈ F(nω₀)·Δω/2π — coefficient per sliver of frequency, not a value at a point
F(ω) equals cₙ exactly at integer ω
F(ω) is the derivative of cₙ
There is no relationship; the transform is a separate theory
feedback: Right — each cₙ shrinks like 1/T, so the honest limit object is amplitude *per unit frequency*: a density, like mass giving way to mass-density for a continuous rod.
cₙ → 0 individually as T grows; F(ω) stays finite precisely because it's the rescaled (×T) version — they can't be equal.
No differentiation is involved in the passage — it's a rescale-and-refine limit, the same one that turns Riemann sums into integrals.
The transform IS the series' limit — same extraction integral, same reconstruction, with Σ ripened into ∫.

questions.prompt: A 1 μs pulse and a 1 s pulse of the same shape: which has the wider spectrum, and why?
options: The 1 s pulse — more signal, more frequencies
The 1 μs pulse — compressing in time stretches in frequency; fast features demand high-frequency content
Both the same — spectrum width depends only on pulse shape
Neither has a spectrum — single pulses aren't periodic
feedback: Duration adds energy, not bandwidth — the long, slow pulse is built comfortably from low frequencies alone.
Right — time-scaling by a reciprocally scales the spectrum by 1/a. It's the c06 lesson (sharp = high-frequency) in transform clothing, and the seed of the uncertainty principle.
Shape sets the spectrum's *profile*; the time-scale sets its *width*. Squeeze one domain and the other bulges — that trade is inescapable.
Escaping periodicity was this concept's whole point: the transform assigns a (continuous) spectrum to any finite-energy one-off signal.

preface.hook: Play three piano keys at once and the air carries one wobbly wave. Your ear pulls the three notes back out of it.
body: Sound reaches you as a single squiggle — air pressure going up and down. When a whole orchestra plays, that is still just one squiggle arriving at your eardrum. Somehow you hear a violin and a drum separately, out of one wiggling line.

That is possible because a complicated wave can always be built by stacking simple ones. Pure tones, each a smooth repeating wave, added together. Get the right ingredients at the right loudnesses and you can rebuild any repeating shape at all.

It works in reverse too, and that is the useful direction. Hand over a messy wave and there is a procedure that tells you exactly which pure tones went into it, and how much of each. You can take the recipe back out of the cake.

This turns out to be one of the most useful ideas anyone has ever had. Your phone compresses music by finding tones your ear will not miss and throwing them away. Noise-cancelling headphones find the rumble and play its exact opposite. Doctors read heart traces this way.
Even a square-cornered wave — up, flat, straight down — can be built from smooth round tones, if you are willing to stack up enough of them. That one seems impossible until you watch it happen.

aha.title: Your ear does this in real time
aha.text: Inside your ear is a coiled tube, and different spots along it respond to different pitches. It physically splits the incoming squiggle into ingredient tones before your brain gets involved. The mathematics was worked out long after the ear was doing it.

aha.title: Sharp corners cost a lot
aha.text: Smooth waves are cheap to build from a few tones. Sharp edges need very many, and no matter how many you add, a small overshoot stays at the corner. That stubborn little wobble has a name and it shows up in real recordings.

aha.title: It is why files can shrink
aha.text: Music and photos compress because most of the ingredients contribute almost nothing that a person would notice. Find those, drop them, keep the rest. That is roughly what MP3 and JPEG are doing.

preface.closer: Any repeating shape is a stack of simple waves, waiting to be listed.
